learning_objective: 🎯 Discover how our eyes and ears gather data, how we focus our attention, and how our brain interprets this raw data to make sense of the world!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Sensation is the process of receiving stimulus energies from the external environment through our sense organs (eyes, ears, skin, nose, tongue).
We are bombarded with stimuli, so we filter them. Selective Attention focuses on one thing while ignoring others. Sustained Attention is maintaining focus on a task over a long period.
Perception is the brain's process of organizing and interpreting sensory information to give it meaning. Sensation is 'hearing a sound'; perception is recognizing it as 'a dog barking'.
Our brain organizes parts into meaningful wholes. Key principles include Figure-Ground (separating object from background), Proximity (grouping close things), and Closure (filling in gaps).
Illusions are misperceptions resulting from a misinterpretation of information received by our sensory organs. They show us that perception is constructive, not a perfect recording.

fun_activity.title: 🌀 The Blind Spot Test
fun_activity.instructions: Draw a small dot and a plus sign (+) about 3 inches apart on a paper. Close your right eye, look at the plus sign with your left eye, and slowly move the paper toward your face. At a certain point, the dot will magically disappear! This is your optic nerve's blind spot.

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly differentiate Sensation (gathering raw data) and Perception (interpreting the data).
📌 Memorize the Gestalt principles of perceptual organization (Proximity, Similarity, Continuity, Closure).
📌 Understand the 'Absolute Threshold': the minimum amount of stimulus energy required to be detected 50% of the time.
quick_recap: ⭐ The human eye has rods (for dim light and black/white vision) and cones (for bright light and color vision).
⭐ Divided attention is when we try to focus on two or more tasks simultaneously (like driving and talking).
⭐ Depth perception relies on both binocular cues (using two eyes) and monocular cues (using one eye).
